e.etymology: From the German occupational surname Fischer, fisherman, the counterpart of English Fisher. Its use as a first name is recent and mostly American.
A modern American combination of Ava and Lee, following the pattern of Emmalee and Annalee.
A respelling of cashmere, the soft goat wool named for the Kashmir region of South Asia, in line with names like Kash and Kashton. Kashmir is the more common spelling for boys.

e.meaning: hero, a person admired for courage
e.etymology: In Greek myth Hero was the priestess loved by Leander, and Shakespeare gave the name to a heroine of Much Ado About Nothing. American parents now use it mostly for boys, from the English word.
namesakes: Hero Fiennes Tiffin (actor in the After film series)

assoc.t: Hero in Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing
hero, a regional word for a sub sandwich

e.note: The Hero of Greek myth and Shakespeare is a woman; in the US the name now goes mostly to boys.

e.etymology: A recent American coinage with no established source, built on the Ny- opening of Nyla and Nyah and the -ari ending of Amari and Kamari.
An American spelling of Keon that came into use in the 1970s and peaked around 2002. Its source is unclear; it follows the sound of Deon and Leon.
The form of Solomon used in Spanish, French, German and Dutch, from Hebrew Shelomoh, built on shalom, peace. Solomon was the wise king of Israel who built the First Temple.

assoc.t: Salomon, ski and trail running gear brand

e.etymology: The West African form of Amina, from Arabic amin, trustworthy. Aminah was the mother of the Prophet Muhammad. The name is common in Senegal, Mali, Guinea and the Gambia.
An Italian diminutive of Gianna, itself short for Giovanna, the feminine of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. In the US it is used mostly by Spanish-speaking families.
A pet form of Elizabeth, clipped to Bet and given the affectionate -sy ending, in use since the 1700s. Elizabeth comes from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath.
namesakes: Betsy Ross (credited with sewing the first American flag)
Betsy DeVos (US secretary of education, 2017 to 2021)

assoc.t: Betsy Ross, credited with sewing the first US flag
Hurricane Betsy, which flooded New Orleans in 1965

e.etymology: The English word, from Old French precios and Latin pretiosus, of great price. Long a term of endearment, it entered the US top 1,000 for girls in 1978 and stayed in the top 500 from 1987 to 2002.

assoc.t: title character of the 2009 film Precious
Gollum's my precious in The Lord of the Rings

e.etymology: An American coinage of the 1990s, built from the Da- prefix of names like Davon and Deshawn and the name Marion, or as a longer form of Damari.
The German, Polish and Scandinavian spelling of Conrad, from Old High German kuoni, bold, and rat, counsel. Saint Conrad of Constance, a 10th-century bishop, helped spread it across the German lands.
namesakes: Konrad Adenauer (first chancellor of West Germany)

e.etymology: A spelling of Amina, from Arabic amin, trustworthy or faithful. Aminah bint Wahb was the mother of the Prophet Muhammad, which keeps the name in steady use among Muslim families.
A recent American coinage combining Jae with -lani, the Hawaiian word for sky or heaven heard in Leilani and Kailani. It also echoes the Swahili name Jelani.
An African American coinage of the 1970s and 1980s that joins the popular Ja- prefix to Quan, a sound also heard in Daquan and Shaquan. It is often written JaQuan or Ja'Quan.
A Spanish short form of Hernando, the older Castilian form of Fernando, from a Visigothic name usually read as journey plus daring. The conquistador Hernán Cortés is the best-known bearer.
namesakes: Hernán Cortés (Spanish conquistador who overthrew the Aztec Empire)

e.etymology: The South Slavic, Ukrainian and Finnish form of Mark, from the Roman name Marcus, probably derived from Mars, the god of war. Prince Marko is the great hero of Serbian epic poetry.
From Arabic salman, safe or sound, from the same s-l-m root as salam, peace. Salman the Persian was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad, which made the name widespread among Muslims.
namesakes: Salman Rushdie (novelist, Midnight's Children and The Satanic Verses)
e.note: Often misread as SAL-mun, which is close to the fish salmon.

e.etymology: Created by Chrétien de Troyes for a Grail knight in his 12th-century romance, shaped like Old French percer val, pierce the valley, and probably adapting the Welsh hero name Peredur.
namesakes: Sir Percival (Knight of the Round Table who seeks the Holy Grail)

assoc.t: Arthurian knight of the Holy Grail quest

e.etymology: From Arabic nur, light, with a feminine ending. Noura is the spelling favored in the Gulf states and North Africa; Nura and the Arabic Nora are the same name.
From Hebrew Uzziyahu, my strength is Yahweh. Uzziah was a king of Judah who reigned for 52 years in the 8th century BC; Isaiah's great vision is dated to the year he died.
namesakes: Uzziah (king of Judah in the Old Testament)
e.note: The natural nickname Uzi is also the name of a submachine gun.

e.etymology: A respelling of Luka, the Slavic form of Luke, from Greek Loukas, man from Lucania in southern Italy. The added h follows Noah, Micah and Jonah.
A creative spelling of Journey, the English word, from Old French jornee, a day's travel. Journey became a girls' name in the 2000s and has many respellings.

assoc.t: sounds like Journey, the band of Don't Stop Believin'

e.etymology: From Sanskrit vani, speech, voice or eloquence, and a name of Saraswati, the goddess of learning and music. Vaani is the spelling that shows the long first vowel.

A spelling of Dominic shaped by Italian Domenico, from Latin Dominicus, belonging to the Lord. It was traditionally given to boys born on Sunday and honors Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican order.
From Hebrew shirah, meaning song or poetry. It is a modern Hebrew name and was the second most popular name for girls born in Israel in 2012.
namesakes: Shira Haas (Israeli actress, star of Unorthodox)

e.etymology: A French pet name for names with a G sound, such as Georgine, Gilberte and Virginie, made famous by Colette's 1944 novella Gigi and the 1958 film. In Italy Gigi is a boys' nickname for Luigi.
namesakes: Gigi (title character of Colette's novella and the 1958 film musical)

assoc.t: common pet name for a grandmother

e.note: Gigi is a popular grandmother name in the US, so many people will hear it as Grandma.

e.etymology: An American coinage of the 2000s that puts a Z on the sound of Aniya, Saniya and Taniya. Zaniyah is the more common spelling.
From Arabic asil, meaning original, genuine or of noble descent, a word also used for purebred Arabian horses. It is given to both girls and boys.
A K spelling of Callan, an Irish surname from Ó Cathaláin, descendant of Cathalán, a pet form of Cathal, battle ruler. It rides the popularity of Kellan and Kallen.
A respelling of Honesty, the English virtue word, from Latin honestas, honor. The -i ending follows names like Majesti and Destini; it is used mainly by African American families.
